Revenge
ree-VENJ
n. and v.
From Old French revenger, from Latin re and vindicare, to claim, to avenge. Webster 1828 distinguishes it sharply from vengeance: revenge is the private return of injury for injury, malicious and forbidden; vengeance is the just infliction of punishment by lawful authority.

Biblical Definition

Revenge in the Authorized Version follows a distinction the modern ear has lost. Where the word describes what God does, it is righteous: God is jealous, and the LORD revengeth; the LORD revengeth, and is furious; the LORD will take vengeance on his adversaries, and he reserveth wrath for his enemies (Nahum 1:2). The triple repetition is not excess but emphasis, opening a book about the destruction of Nineveh. Where the word describes a believer’s zeal against sin discovered in himself, it is commended: Paul lists the fruits of the Corinthians’ godly sorrow and ends with it — what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge! (2 Corinthians 7:11). The revenge is against their own former negligence, not against a person. A prophet may ask God to take up his cause: remember me, and visit me, and revenge me of my persecutors (Jeremiah 15:15). But private retaliation between men is flatly forbidden: Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD (Leviticus 19:18).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines REVENGE as the return of an injury for an injury, with malice or resentment — a private act, and always criminal in the individual; distinguished from vengeance, the just infliction of punishment by lawful authority or by God.

expand to see more

REVENGE, n. — The return of an injury for an injury, in resentment; the deliberate infliction of pain or evil in retaliation.

REVENGE, v.t. — To inflict pain or injury in return for an injury received; to vindicate by punishment.

In the individual, revenge is always criminal, being the effect of malice; God has reserved vengeance to Himself and to the magistrate.

To revenge a cause, in Scripture, is to take up and vindicate the cause of another, as when God avenges His people.

From Latin re and vindico, to claim, to avenge — the root also of vengeance, avenge, and vindicate.

Key Scripture

Nahum 1:2 — "God is jealous, and the LORD revengeth; the LORD revengeth, and is furious; the LORD will take vengeance on his adversaries, and he reserveth wrath for his enemies."

2 Corinthians 7:11 — "For behold this selfsame thing, that ye sorrowed after a godly sort, what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge! In all things ye have approved yourselves to be clear in this matter."

Leviticus 19:18 — "Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD."

Romans 12:19 — "Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord."

Modern Corruption

Romans 12:19 forbids private revenge on the ground that God will certainly repay, so that the modern reading of forgiveness as the release of the offender from all reckoning removes the very reason the command gives.

expand to see more

Paul’s logic is exact and it is often reversed. Avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord. The reason the Christian may lay down retaliation is that the debt will be collected by a better Creditor. The modern account of forgiveness usually says the opposite — that letting go means deciding the wrong no longer counts, or that it was smaller than it felt, or that the offender was doing his best. Scripture never asks a wronged person to revise the size of the wrong. It asks him to hand the case to a court that will not fail, which is possible precisely because judgment is real. Hebrews 10:30 repeats the quotation, and Revelation 6:10 has the martyrs asking how long without rebuke.

2 Corinthians 7:11 shows the one direction in which the church may safely turn this energy: against its own sin. The Corinthians had tolerated a scandal; when Paul’s letter produced godly sorrow, it produced indignation, fear, vehement desire, zeal, and revenge — a settled hostility toward what they had permitted. That is what repentance looks like in a congregation, and it is unmistakably fiercer than the modern process of acknowledging that mistakes were made. Nahum 1:2 supplies the ground beneath both: God is jealous and He repays. A God who did not would leave the wronged with nothing but their own hands.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew naqam (H5358), to avenge; neqamah (H5360), vengeance; Greek ekdikesis (G1557), vindication, vengeance; ekdikeo (G1556), to vindicate; orge (G3709), wrath.

expand to see more

Hebrew naqam (H5358) — to avenge, to take vengeance; the LORD revengeth (Nahum 1:2).

Hebrew neqamah (H5360) — vengeance; To me belongeth vengeance (Deuteronomy 32:35), the verse Paul quotes.

Greek ekdikesis (G1557) — the carrying out of justice; Vengeance is mine; I will repay (Romans 12:19).

Greek ekdikesis in 2 Corinthians 7:11 — rendered revenge, of the church’s zeal against its own tolerated sin.

Greek orge (G3709) — settled wrath; the wrath to which Paul says the believer is to give place.

Usage

"The LORD revengeth, and is furious (Nahum 1:2) — the just repayment that belongs to God alone."

"What zeal, yea, what revenge! (2 Corinthians 7:11) — a church turning this energy against its own tolerated sin."

"Avenge not yourselves… Vengeance is mine (Romans 12:19) — retaliation laid down because the debt will be collected."
